An employee complained that his employer, a utility company, did not properly answer his access request for the data it used to bring a disciplinary charge against him. The charge was based on a private investigator's report, which he only learned of during his dismissal court case. The company first treated the request as one for access to the work computer, then called it generic and refused it. The Garante found breaches of fairness (Art. 5(1)(a)), Art. 12 and Art. 15, rejected the 'minor infringement' argument, and fined the company EUR 10,000, with publication of the decision.

Data collected for a risk assessment for vaccination against Monkeypox was considered a violation of the principles of lawfulness, fairness and transparency and of integrity and confidentiality (Article 5(1)(a), Article 5(1)(f) and Article 13 GDPR).

The Icelandic DPA fined the Office of the National Medical Examiner ISK 12,000,000 (approx. € 82,000) for multiple GDPR violations after a security breach on its website Heilsuvera – an online healthcare system and prescription portal.

The Swedish DPA held that by using Google Analytics provided by Google LLC, Tele2 Sverige breached Article 44 GDPR. SCCs and safeguards that were in place could not support data transfers to the US in a way that would not undermine the level of protection of personal data guaranteed by the GDPR.

IMY investigated a complaint, passed on from the Austrian authority, about CDON AB's website using Google Analytics. Through the tool, visitors' personal data was transferred to the USA. IMY found that the data was personal data, that CDON was the controller, and that the standard contractual clauses and CDON's supplementary measures (such as IP truncation) did not ensure the protection level required by Chapter V. It found a breach of Article 44 GDPR. It fined CDON SEK 300,000 and ordered it to bring its use of Google Analytics into line with Chapter V, in particular by stopping use of the version in use on 14 August 2020 unless sufficient safeguards are put in place.

The Swedish DPA held that by using Google Analytics provided by Google LLC, Coop breached Article 44 GDPR. SCCs and safeguards that were in place could not support data transfers to the US in a way that would not undermine the level of protection of personal data guaranteed by the GDPR.

The Swedish DPA held that by using Google Analytics provided by Google LLC, Dagens Industri breached Article 44 GDPR. SCCs and safeguards that were in place could not support data transfers to the US in a way that would not undermine the level of protection of personal data guaranteed by the GDPR.

A gynaecologist replied publicly to a patient's critical online review and revealed her diagnosis. The reply stayed visible at least until 3 October 2022. The Austrian DPA found that this was unlawful processing of health data and breached the principles of lawfulness, purpose limitation and data minimisation. It held the act was intentional. It imposed a fine of EUR 10,000 (336 hours substitute imprisonment) plus EUR 1,000 procedural costs, using an estimated income because he did not disclose his finances.

The DPA held that Google must delete nine specified links from its search results under Article 17 GDPR, as the data subject's “particular situation” outweighed public interest. Furthermore, the DPA confirmed its jurisdiction despite Google having no EU establishment.

The DPA ordered Google to delete links appearing in search results for the data subject's name. Additionally, the DPA ordered Google to amend it's deletion request process by enabling the submission of attachments, providing direct contact information and ceasing automated responses.

The DPA reprimanded a controller for not providing access to all data processed about the data subject. The controller explained how to request the missing data, but the DPA considered this procedure overly complicated.
The Spanish DPA fined a controller €2,000 for infringing Article 13 GDPR in their contract with a tenant.

Persónuvernd published a summary of its decision of 2 May 2023 closing a security audit of the Icelandic Health Insurance agency. The agency had fixed the issues it was ordered to correct. Two serious weaknesses existing at the time of the on-site inspection, lack of multi-factor authentication for staff and healthcare providers accessing health data systems and use of real data in development and test environments, were found to breach Articles 5(1)(f), 32 and 25 GDPR. An administrative fine of ISK 2 million was imposed. The fine decision and the audit decision themselves are not published for information security reasons.

According to the Belgian DPA, a US-based controller whose activity includes the organisation of conferences in Europe is subject to the GDPR and must, among other obligations, appoint a representative.

The Romanian supervisory authority investigated Farmacia Ardealul SRL after the company notified a personal data security breach. Malware had been installed on the company's website, and a fake bank-data collection form was added, compromising the bank data of a significant number of customers. The authority found that the company had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational measures for the risk, as required by Article 32(1)(b), (d) and (2) GDPR. It imposed a fine of 12,424 lei (about EUR 2,500) and a corrective measure requiring a plan for periodic testing and assessment of the security of all its IT systems, including the website.

A debt collection company sent default information on small consumer loans issued by a Danish lender to the credit bureau Creditinfo Lánstraust. The loan terms lacked the required clause permitting default registration, and some claims were below the minimum amount allowed for registration. About 2,000 people were affected. Persónuvernd found the processing had no legal basis and breached the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle, and fined the company ISK 3,500,000. The company did not respond to the authority's letters.

Persónuvernd examined how eCommerce 2020 ApS, a Danish small-loan company, sent loan defaults to the Icelandic credit bureau Creditinfo Lánstraust. Between July 2018 and May 2019 its loan terms lacked the required clause allowing default registration, and claims below the minimum amount (577 individuals) were also reported. The authority held that the company was the controller and had no valid legal basis, and breached the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle. It imposed an administrative fine of ISK 7,500,000, taking into account the number of data subjects (about 2,000), the burdensome nature of the processing and the company's reduced activity.

The Icelandic DPA ruled on a complaint by the Consumers' Association about the credit bureau Creditinfo Lánstraust hf. registering defaults on small loans granted by eCommerce 2020 ApS. The bureau recorded the claims although the loan terms lacked the clause required by its operating licence for registering defaults, and some claims were below the minimum amount. It had not adequately checked that the registration conditions were met and deleted the entries late. The DPA found a breach of lawfulness and accountability and fined the company ISK 37,856,900, 2.5% of its 2021 turnover.
The DPA fined a media company SEK 13,000,000 for unlawfully profiling its users in order to target them with behavioral advertising on its website, thus violating Article 6(1) GDPR.
The DPA reprimanded a controller for not appropriately clarifying whether its processing operations were based on consent or a contract.

Due to an error within a digital identity solution used nationwide, several citizens accidentally gained access to bank accounts of another person. The Danish DPA held that only recommending and not requiring a mandatory validation of tokens for the safe use, which would eliminate the error, the solution violated Article 32 GDPR.

The Belgian DPA confirmed that CCTV images made to protect against littering and illegal dumping can be used to fine a data subject doing the littering, based on public interest under Article 6(1)(e) GDPR. The DPA also noted that person combining the roles of DPO and safety consultant could pose a breach of Article 38(6) GDPR.

The Italian DPA imposed a fine of €1,000,000 on Autostrade per l'Italia for erroneously indicating the developer of a toll reimbursement app as the controller. The DPA also found a violation of the principles of lawfulness and transparency.

Digi reported a data breach in September 2019: an attacker exploited a years-old known vulnerability in its content management system on digi.hu and reached databases of about 322,000 people, mostly a test database that should have been deleted after use. The authority had fined Digi HUF 100 million in 2020; after the CJEU (C-77/21) and the Budapest Tribunal found no purpose-limitation violation, the authority repeated the procedure on the sanctions. It found violations of storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e)) and security of processing (Art. 32(1)-(2)), ordered Digi to review all its databases for the need for encryption, and fined it HUF 80 million (4/5 of the original). The decision is to be published with the controller's identity.
The Hungarian DPA reduced a fine issued in response to data breach from 100,000,000 HUF to 80,000,000 HUF (equivalent to €200,000) following a re-evaluation after CJEU decision Case C-77/21.

On the basis of the Austrian data protection law implementing Article 89 GDPR, the Austrian DPA held that processing activities supporting scientific research in the field of automated driving shall be authorised by the supervisory authority itself.

The Polish DPA was handling a complaint about a company passing a person's data to a third party without a legal basis. It twice asked the company for explanations, but the company never collected the registered letters, so they were deemed delivered, and it never answered. The DPA opened separate proceedings and found that the company breached Article 58(1)(a) and (e) GDPR by not giving the authority access to the information it needed. It imposed an administrative fine of PLN 33,012 (about EUR 7,000), citing the continuing, negligent failure and complete lack of cooperation.

The DPA reprimanded an employer for the usage of vague language in its privacy policy creating the false impression that the processing of employment data is based on consent rather than the performance of the employment contract.
The Spanish DPA fined a logistics company €50,000 for installing videocameras in the employees' rest area, in violation of Article 6 GDPR.

Romania's ANSPDCP, acting as lead authority after the Hungarian DPA referred three complaints against Dante International SA (the emag online shop), found that the company failed to facilitate and honour erasure requests, gave incomplete information on third-country transfers, and kept using a complainant's email address without consent. It fined the company RON 148,830 (EUR 30,000) for Articles 12(2) and 17(1) and RON 49,610 (EUR 10,000) for Article 6(1)(a), and issued a warning for Articles 13 and 14. It also ordered corrective measures: complete privacy information, an anonymisation method, and regular staff training across the group.
The Belgian DPA decided that subjective statements made in a meeting and faithfully recorded in the minutes do not fall within the scope of Article 16 GDPR.

A pharmacist complained to the Belgian DPA that the Order of Pharmacists kept data about a disciplinary sanction imposed on him and refused his erasure request. The Litigation Chamber found that the processing infringed the principles of Article 5(1)(a) to (e) GDPR, among other things because the Order never checked whether the sanction, based on the old code of ethics, was still accurate and relevant after the new code was adopted. It fined the Order EUR 30,000 (reduced from the EUR 50,000 first proposed), ordered erasure of the sanction data from the complainant's disciplinary file and ordered the Order to bring its processing into line with Article 5(1). The decision is published with the Order identified.
The Irish DPA fined the Department of Health €22,500 for processing personal data from people involved in litigation against it in an unsafe, excessive and non-transparent manner.
The Austrian DPA issued a €1,000 monetary penalty against a controller for unlawfully further processing personal data in breach of Article 6(4) GDPR. The further purpose was political advertisement.

The French DPA approved a draft decree and data protection impact assessment carried out by the French Ministry of Interior. The draft decree outlined plans for the development and implementation of a system of algorithmic processing of images collected by aerial video surveillance, to be used during the 2024 Olympic Games for the purpose of identifying terrorism risks.

The Romanian authority finished an investigation in May 2023 into Artima S.A., started after a personal data breach notification. Employees filmed the video surveillance monitor with their personal phones, and one passed the footage to an outsider who posted it on Facebook. The authority found the company had not put in place adequate technical and organisational security measures. It fined the company 39,712 lei (about EUR 8,000) and ordered it to implement a solution to monitor application of its existing work procedures.

The Greek DPA held that genealogical research on a family surname did not fall within the scope of Article 15 GDPR, as "personal data concerning [the data subject]," because the data subject requested access to the Directorate's entire database (containing other data subject's personal data), not access to data directly relating to him.

The Icelandic DPA held that recording a neighbor’s private conversation and sending the audio recording to the neighbor, with regard to a dispute between the neighbors, falls within the so-called “house exemption” pursuant to Article 2(2)(c) GDPR.

The Hellenic DPA accepted the complaint in which the data subject complained about Google's refusal to delete search results that appeared based on her name. The data subject claimed that because of the results of the search engine for several years she was unable to find a job, while she added that keeping them has a negative effect on her professional carrer.

A complaint aiming at ordering the restitution of a file from a lawyer to its client is not an Article 15 GDPR matter. The DPA considered that it was clear from the facts that this matter concerned lawyers professional conduct and that it had, in any case, no competence to order the restitution of the file

An employee using a personal phone to take pictures of an asylum seeker's social medias to use it in the asylum procedure is not violating the GDPR, even if the asylum office prohibited the use of private devices at work.

The DPA dismissed the data subject's complaint about their data not being deleted from the Austrian Justice System (Verfahrensautomation der Justiz) as it has no supervisory authority over data processed in the course of judicial activities.

IMY examined how Spotify handles data subjects' right of access, both its general procedures and three complaints forwarded from other EU authorities. It found that the information Spotify gave under Article 15(1)(a-h) and 15(2), and its description of the technical log files, was not clear or specific enough. IMY imposed an administrative fine of SEK 58 million, treating the infringements as low in gravity given the very high turnover of the parent group. For two complaints it found minor infringements and issued a reprimand, and ordered Spotify to give one complainant access. The third complaint was rejected, and the Danish authority is to adopt that part.

The Hellenic DPA fined a bank €210,000 for mistakenly including its customers's personal data in a list of debtors and for not properly responding to an access request. The DPA also concluded that the controller did not implement sufficient organizational and technical measures according to Article 25 GDPR.

A customer complained that a store employee of the Rinascente department store had altered her loyalty-card name to an offensive one. The Garante then inspected the company's marketing and profiling activity. It archived most of the objections: the complainant's data breach, the notice given to her, the single declaration of will, and the Facebook-Meta campaigns. It found violations on a second data breach (70 orders e-mailed to 5 wrong customers), on the 7-year retention of marketing data and the vague retention information, and on the missing data protection impact assessment before profiling. It ordered differentiated retention periods and imposed a fine of EUR 300,000, with the decision published.

A woman complained to the Garante about the weekly magazine 'Oggi', published by RCS Mediagroup, which printed photographs of her at home, taken from the street with a zoom lens months earlier, showing a private moment of intimacy. The Garante found that the photos were collected with invasive techniques and that their publication was excessive and not essential to the journalistic purpose, even though she is a public figure. It held that this breached the principles of fairness, transparency and data minimisation in Article 5(1)(a) and (c) GDPR, read with the journalism provisions of the Italian Code and the ethical rules. It banned any further dissemination of the photos, including online and in the historical archive, and fined the publisher EUR 40,660.
The Italian DPA issued a fine of €30,000 to a local newspaper for publishing a minor’s data.

The Garante inspected Istat's SIM (Sistema di Integrazione dei Microdati) system, which pseudonymises microdata used for statistical integration, to check compliance with its January 2020 provision on the census. The inspection found that the pseudonymisation, data classification and singularity controls were still not adequate, and Istat's own documents admitted a total compromise of the database if one unit were breached. The Garante declared the processing unlawful under Articles 5(2), 24, 25 and 32 GDPR and issued a reprimand, but imposed no fine because it considered the violations minor and Istat cooperative. It ordered Istat to bring the processing into compliance within 180 days and to report on the measures taken.
The Spanish DPA fined a company €2,000 after noyb submitted a cookie complaint over the installation of non-essential cookies and flawed consent practices in relation a cookie banner.
The Slovenian DPA ruled out a breach of Article 32 GDPR since the concerned data, a phone number used by a company, was not "personal" under Article 4(1) GDPR.

The Polish data protection authority was handling a complaint about a company disclosing a person's phone number to unauthorised parties. The company ignored two formal requests for explanations, so the authority opened a separate procedure of its own motion. It found that the company breached Article 31 and Article 58(1)(a) and (e) GDPR by not cooperating and not giving the authority the information it needed. It imposed an administrative fine of PLN 18,864 (about EUR 4,000), set on an estimated basis because the company supplied no financial data. The decision is stated to be final.

The Belgian DPA dismissed a complaint based on article 95, §1, 3 LCA because the data subject did not adequately prove a breach of the GDPR. The Belgian DPA stated that it would require a disproportionate amount of resources, compared to the limited impact, to resolve the issue.
An employer, informing the staff of the dismissal of some employees together with the reasons of the dismissal, breached the principle of data minimisation of Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.

A former employee of the Comune di Napoli complained that the council, by mistake, sent one email to her and two other former employees attaching their performance evaluations and a ranking with scores. The council said the mistake was human error and that it had sent the documents by email because staff were short during the COVID-19 emergency. The Garante held that the communication to third parties had no legal basis and breached the principle of lawfulness and Articles 5(1)(a) and 6 GDPR and Article 2-ter of the Codice. It imposed a fine of EUR 3,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

An employee-related report alleged that an Italian company used a recording CCTV camera without notice, fingerprint readers to arm its alarm, and a GPS tracking app on technicians' phones. After an inspection by the Guardia di Finanza, the Garante found that the company processed employees' biometric data without a legal basis, tracked technicians' location continuously and excessively, and ran a camera without the union agreement or labour inspectorate authorisation required by Article 4 of the Workers' Statute. Information given to staff was inadequate in all three cases (oral only). The Garante banned the CCTV processing and the continuous tracking of workers' location, fined the company EUR 20,000, and ordered publication of the decision. The alleged breach of Article 6 was dropped.

A complainant received appointment reminder SMS messages and found invoices for medical services in his pre-filled tax return that were not his. The medical centre had mixed up two patients with the same name and put the complainant's tax code and address on the other patient's invoices. The Garante found breaches of accuracy, integrity and confidentiality, the rules on health data and security, and fined the centre EUR 10,000. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ended and the centre had put safeguards in place. The decision is to be published in full.

A complaint reached the Garante about an advertising poster put up by the Tuscany South-East local health authority, showing a healthcare worker at a workstation where a patient's name appeared on an emergency room record on screen. The poster hung for a few weeks in the main patient entrance corridor of the emergency department, an area accessible to anyone. The Garante found this was a dissemination of health data in breach of the data protection principles, Articles 9 and 25 GDPR and Article 2-septies(8) of the Italian Code. It imposed a fine of EUR 20,000 and ordered publication of the decision, but no corrective measures because the poster had already been removed. Mitigating factors included prompt cooperation, staff training and a new internal procedure.

A job candidate asked the employment agency Cooperjob to delete his personal data and received no reply within the one-month deadline. The company only deleted the data and answered after the Garante intervened. The Garante found a breach of Articles 12(3) and 17 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 20,000, and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

A security company's electronic licensing documentation, containing personal data of security staff and contracting individuals, was encrypted in a ransomware attack. The company neither notified the supervisory authority within 72 hours nor informed the affected people, although the authority had pointed it to its obligations. The authority found breaches of integrity and accountability, of data protection by design, of security of processing, and of the breach notification duties. It imposed a fine of PLN 47,160, equal to EUR 10,000. It found only aggravating or neutral factors and no mitigating ones.

The Commissioner has issued a reprimand to Thames Valey Police (TVP) in accordance with Schedule 13(2)(c) of the Data Protection Act 2018 (DPA 2018) in respect of appropriate security principle infringements (Law Enforcement Directive case).

The Finnish DPA found a retail chain to have breached Article 5(1)(e) GDPR, Article 25(1) GDPR and Article 25(2) GDPR for its lengthy storage of purchase behaviour data in connection with its loyalty program.

The Hellenic DPA fined a telecommunications company a total of €150,000 for sending unsolicited advertising messages, for not responding to an access request and for not facilitating the objection to processing of personal data.

The Belgian DPA reprimands a supermarket for lack of legal basis to check CCTV images to resolve a customer complaint. The DPA stated that the employees accessing the CCTV also should have received more in-depth training.

The Belgian DPA ordered a ban on the transfer of tax data of US citizens residing in Belgium to the US. According to the DPA the FATCA agreement, which provides for such transfers, is not in line with the GDPR and the Belgian tax authority should have conducted an impact assessment.

The Slovenian DPA ordered a controller to cease using some of the video cameras on the company's premises because video surveillance in, e.g. restrooms and corridors, could not be based on legitimate interest as there is no realistic threat to property or people.
Jigler Payroll B.V. infringed on GDPR article 6, but infringement of GDPR article 28 and 46 could not be established. The AP decided not to take any enforcement action.

The Latvian DPA found the use of a personal unique identifier was insufficient to clearly identify a data subject and prevent unlawful disclosure of special categories of data by the national health service provider. The use of additional criteria, such as the data subject's name, was necessary.
The DPA held that the controller's identity verification requirements for an erasure request should be proportionate to the consequences the data subject could suffer in case of erroneous erasure.

The Andalusian DPA found that an education department lacked a legal basis for recording audio of its meetings. It considered that a national law’s requirement that minutes be documented and that they “may be recorded” did not constitute a legal obligation under Article 6 GDPR.

Romania's data protection authority investigated a car dealer after it notified a personal data breach. Data of 290 customers and prospects (contact details, car and purchase preferences, marketing consents) were publicly accessible on the company's website from July to 4 August 2022. The authority found inadequate security measures (Art. 32) and failure to apply privacy by design and by default (Art. 25). It fined the company RON 88,563.60 (about EUR 18,000) for Art. 32, issued a warning for Art. 25, and ordered a plan for regular testing and evaluation of systems.

A Croatian betting company offered players payout of winnings to VISA cards and, in doing so, collected copies of both sides of their bank cards. After a complaint, the Agency opened an ex officio procedure and found there was no legal basis for collecting the copies, as money laundering rules did not require it. Players were not properly informed, the new payment process lacked suitable technical and organisational measures, and the stored copies were not encrypted or regularly assessed for security. Employees could see the full data on 655 of 2,078 copies. The Agency fined the company EUR 380,000, treating the financial nature of the data as aggravating and the company's prompt remediation as mitigating.

A client of a web and video development company complained that his phone calls with it were recorded and that his request for access to the recordings was refused; the company only offered to let him listen at its offices. The Litigation Chamber found a breach of the right of access (Articles 12(2) and 15 GDPR) and imposed a fine of EUR 40,000, lowered from the EUR 70,000 first proposed. It also issued a reprimand for transparency failings in the privacy statement (unclear language, retention periods not stated) and ordered the company to grant access. Other complaints were dismissed. A note says the Market Court confirmed the decision on 20 December 2023.
The Spanish DPA held that the registration of a data subject in a common credit information system was unlawful as the debt was neither 'certain, nor due or payable'. It fined the controller €50,000.

A customer whose long-term rental financing request was refused complained that Volkswagen Leasing GmbH did not give him the credit-reference report data it obtained from CRIF when he made an access request. The company had only pointed him to CRIF and supplied the report on 19 December 2022, during the proceedings. The Garante found that Articles 12 and 15 GDPR were infringed. It fined the company EUR 40,000 and ordered publication of the decision. It made no order to satisfy the access request, since the company had already complied.

Several patients complained that they had received a letter containing another person's income-based health exemption certificate, and the health authority ULSS 6 Euganea also notified a personal data breach. A mass mailing of about 39,852 exemption certificates went out with the personal data misaligned, because an employee prepared the file in Excel and checked only the first row's preview. The Garante found the processing unlawful for breaching the basic principles in Articles 5 and 6 and the security obligations in Article 32 GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision. It adopted no corrective measures, since the authority had already sent the correct certificates and asked recipients to destroy the wrong ones.

A complainant received unsolicited promotional emails from a small company that had collected professionals' addresses from public lists, and kept receiving them after objecting and asking for deletion. The Garante held that email marketing needs prior consent and that public sources do not remove that requirement, and that the objection and erasure rights were not respected. It banned the company from using for promotion data without proven consent, ordered their deletion, and fined it EUR 10,000, taking into account that it is a micro-enterprise.

Since 2012 the Garante received many complaints about an online phone-directory website, which published people's names, phone numbers and addresses without any legal basis, including unlisted numbers. The site had no identification of its owner, its deletion form did not work, and its consent boxes were pre-ticked and could not be unticked. After long investigations the owner was identified through Google AdSense data. He was already subject to a May 2022 sanction and ban for a similar site. The Garante declared the processing unlawful and banned collecting, keeping and publishing personal data to build an online phone directory not drawn from the national single database (d.b.u.). It fined the operator EUR 60,000, ordered publication of the decision and recorded the violations in its internal register.

A customer complained that Santander Consumer Bank did not properly or timely answer her access request and her request to delete negative credit-bureau information about a loan. The bank had answered late, saying only that the loan had been sold to another company and she should ask that company. The bank argued it was no longer controller and blamed its processor, which the Garante rejected, since answering data subject requests is the controller's duty. Only after the Garante's invitation did the bank supply the data. The Garante found a breach of Article 12(3) and (4) and fined the bank EUR 10,000.

The public prosecutor's office reported that the newspaper La Gazzetta di Parma printed a photo of a murder suspect in handcuffs and physical restraint between two prison police officers, and an online photo with pixelated handcuffs. The Garante found this breached the lawfulness and fairness principle (Art. 5(1)(a) GDPR), the Code, and the journalists' code of conduct, which protect the dignity of detained persons. It took into account the publisher's prompt removal of the images, new internal procedures and admission of error, but also a previous violation by the same publisher. It fined the company EUR 10,000, banned further processing of these or similar images, and ordered publication of the decision.

A German DPA found that a "pay-or-okay" system on the main webpage of a media outlet is, in principle, permissible. However, in the case at hand the legal requirements for obtaining consent were not fulfilled.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in April 2023 into the national postal company. It found that in January 2023 the company partly filled in Form 230 with employees' names and personal ID numbers, so as to redirect 3.5% of their income tax to a foundation belonging to the company. It had no legal obligation or other legal basis for this, such as employee consent. The company was fined 24,719.50 lei (equivalent to EUR 5,000) and recommended to ensure lawful processing in future. The company has paid the fine in full.

Following a complaint by noyb, the Maltese DPA ordered C-Planet to comply with an access request and to inform about the source of the personal data. In the case at hand the data had been exposed in a breach involving the political opinions of 335,000 voters on the island.

This is a DPC press release (dated 22 May 2023) announcing the conclusion of its inquiry into Meta Ireland's transfers of Facebook users' personal data from the EU/EEA to the US. The DPC's final decision of 12 May 2023 found that Meta Ireland infringed Article 46(1) GDPR by continuing transfers after the Schrems II judgment, relying on the 2021 SCCs and supplementary measures that did not address the risks identified by the CJEU. After objections from four concerned authorities, the dispute went to the EDPB under Article 65, which decided on 13 April 2023. The DPC then imposed a EUR 1.2 billion fine and two orders: suspension of future transfers to the US within five months, and bringing processing into compliance with Chapter V by ceasing unlawful storage in the US within six months.

The French DPA fined Doctissimo €380,000 for several data protection violations, including failure to obtain users' consent for the processing of health data, lack of security measures, violation of storage limitation and setting cookies without consent.

The Romanian authority finished an investigation into Libra Internet Bank SA in March 2023, started after a complaint about a refused access request. The bank had not sent a full reply: it gave no copy of the data (a video recording) in the requested form, did not post the reply to the address requested, and did not tell the person about the right to complain or seek a judicial remedy. It also had no measures to make access to video copies easier. The bank was fined two amounts (EUR 1,000 and EUR 10,000 equivalent) and ordered to answer the request in full and adopt technical and organisational measures.
The Austrian DPA found that Clearview AI’s processing activities violated the GDPR. Nevertheless, it did not impose a fine nor ordered the controller to stop the processing.
The Spanish DPA found a violation of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR and fined €2,000 a 'community of owners' for accessing video surveillance footage and sharing it without authorization.
The DPA of Cyprus examined the case of public online disclosure of sensitive personal data of the complainant.

After an anonymous complaint in December 2022 that a USB stick with personal data of 77,317 debtors was circulating, the Croatian authority opened an ex officio supervision of a debt collection agency. It found three violations: unclear information on the legal basis for returning overpaid funds, no processor contract for a bankruptcy monitoring service, and inadequate technical and organisational security measures. The controller was negligent and cooperated poorly. The authority imposed an administrative fine of EUR 2,265,000.

A British resident invited to speak at the Mobile World Congress 2021 in Barcelona complained that in-person registration required uploading passport data for facial recognition by a third-country processor. The AEPD opened proceedings against the organiser GSMA Ltd. and found that it had not carried out a genuine data protection impact assessment before using facial recognition for access; the assessment provided was merely nominal. It imposed a fine of EUR 200,000 for breach of Article 35 GDPR. The decision treated the large number of attendees and a serious lack of diligence as aggravating, and rejected the mitigating arguments raised by GSMA.

The DPA considered that a school informing the pupils' parents that some professors were on strike did not reveal trade union membership and was therefore not a sensitive data under Article 9 GDPR. However, this processing was not necessary to carry out a public task (i.e. the school's education mission) and therefore lacked legal basis.

The Hungarian DPA found that a solarium studio could not rely on legitimate interests under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR without carrying out a balancing of interests test. The DPA also held that the studio violated Articles 13(1)(2) GDPR by only providing the information, on paper and upon request.

The complainant submits a complaint to the DPA after having repeatedly unsuccessfully addressed the controller to exercise his right to data portability in the context of switching to a new health insurance fund. The DPA rejects the complaints since the conditions in order to exercise the right to data portability were not met.

The Belgian DPA considered that a data subject complaining against his former employer for publishing a picture in which he appears lacked standing since he could not prove he was actually on the photo.

During an environmental inspection on a private property, the Guardia di finanza found a video surveillance system with cameras that filmed a public road and neighbouring properties. The controller did not reply to the Garante's requests and did not show any legitimate interest or effective risk justifying that footage. The Garante found breaches of the lawfulness principle and of the legal basis requirement, imposed a fine of EUR 400, and ordered the cameras to be repositioned so that they only cover the owner's own property.

After press reports, the Garante investigated Rome's Flaminio cemetery, where small crosses over buried aborted foetuses carried labels with the names of the women who had terminated a pregnancy and a date. The municipality (Roma Capitale) was the controller and its in-house company AMA S.p.A. the processor. The Garante found that the women's health data were disclosed and that the controller had not given adequate instructions to the processor, and had then implemented its corrective instructions only partly and inadequately. It fined Roma Capitale EUR 176,000 and ordered publication of the decision, but imposed no further corrective measures since the municipality had by then remedied the problems.

After press reports, the Garante found that at the Flaminio cemetery in Rome hundreds of crosses over burials of aborted foetuses carried labels with the names of the women who had terminated a pregnancy. Ama S.p.a., which runs the cemeteries as processor for Roma Capitale, had not asked the controller for instructions despite the legal gaps, and later only partly and inadequately applied the instructions and measures the controller gave. The Garante declared the processing unlawful and fined Ama EUR 239,000, with publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were ordered because Ama had by then replaced the plates and the conduct had exhausted its effects.

A teacher complained that the Lecce school office published on its online notice board a decree assigning substitute-teaching posts, with tables on about 300 teachers that showed whether each had priority under Law 104/1992 (disability or caring status). The office argued that the mention was generic, that it was required for transparency, and that the Covid-19 emergency forced the new online procedure. The Garante found this was unlawful dissemination of personal data, including health data, without a proper legal basis. It fined the office EUR 15,000, banned further online dissemination of the data, required a report on measures taken within 30 days, and ordered publication of the decision.

Following a Guardia di finanza inspection on 11 May 2022, the Garante found that a sole trader wholesaling non-ferrous metals had four operating CCTV cameras at its premises without the required information signs. The sole trader claimed the signs had been removed only temporarily and later reinstated, with photos. The Garante found the temporary-removal claim unsupported by objective evidence but took the later installation into account. It found breaches of the transparency principle (Article 5(1)(a)) and the information obligation (Article 13), imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

The Italian DPA fined Benetton Group €240,000 for storing consumer data for an excessive period and illegally using it for marketing and profiling purposes. The DPA also held that the company did not implement sufficient measures to ensure the security of the data.

A former contract lecturer complained that the university disclosed data about a criminal proceeding against him. The disclosures were made in notes to the Labour Inspectorate, to the Public Function Inspectorate and to all Italian university rectors. The university argued that the notes contained no criminal-offence data and that it was defending its rights and reputation. The Garante found the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a), 6 and 10 GDPR and Articles 2-ter and 2-octies of the Code. It fined the university EUR 4,000 and ordered publication of the decision. It adopted no further corrective measures because the conduct had ceased.

Three former employees complained that their company, Geico S.p.A., kept their work email accounts active after their employment ended, redirected them and accessed their content, then used the emails in court proceedings against them, without giving them any information. The Garante found that the company's policies did not tell employees about such processing after termination. It found breaches of the basic principles (fairness, purpose limitation, minimisation, storage limitation, integrity and confidentiality) and of the duty to inform. It fined the company EUR 40,000 and ordered publication of the decision.
The ICO has issued a formal reprimand to the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) after confidential waste documents were left in an unsecured prison holding area.
The Finnish DPA ordered the controller to delete all personal data that were transferred without a lawful basis to the United States by use of Google Analytics and reCAPTCHA services.

The Norwegian DPA imposed a ban on the national statistical institute's planned real-time mass-processing of nearly all purchase data in the country, including linkage to bank accounts and birth dates, for the purpose of providing official statistics.

An employee of Region Skåne forgot an unencrypted USB stick in the pocket of clinical clothes sent to the laundry. It held personal identity numbers and health data on 1,934 patients from a quality register, and it was never found. IMY held that the region had not ensured a security level appropriate to the risk and so breached Article 32(1) GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of SEK 200,000. The region's argument that the breach was only down to one employee's negligence was rejected, because the controller is responsible for processing within its activities.

The Norwegian Privacy Appeals Board found that a car rental platform had a legal basis under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR to assess the credit of a data subject in order to reduce the company's financial risk.

The Danish DPA reprimanded a controller for sharing personal data with Meta Ireland without prior ascertaining that the latter complied with the GDPR when transferring data to Meta Platforms in the US.

The Belgian DPA dismissed a request to erasure based on Article 17(3) GDPR because of reasons of public interest in the field of public health in according with Article 9(2)(h)GDPR. It is not up the DPA to determine the correctness of an opinion written by a care provider in light of child protection services regarding the mental well-being of both the child and the mother.

The Belgian DPA dismissed a complaint based on technical reasons regarding unlawful processing of personal data sent via e-mails concerning supplementary pension from a third intermediate party to an insurance company, instructed by complainant's former employer, .

The Italian Garante investigated Green Network S.p.A. after complaints and reports of unsolicited promotional calls made in its name, some to numbers in the public opt-out register. It found that the company had not shown effective oversight of calls made in its name by its sales network, breaching accountability and data protection by design. It ordered the company to align its sales network processes and to control access to the contract activation platform, and imposed a fine of EUR 237,800 plus publication of the decision.

The Garante investigated energy supplier Sorgenia after a complaint and several reports about unwanted promotional calls made in its name, some to numbers in the public opt-out register, and about unanswered erasure/objection requests. It found Sorgenia had not shown accountability or privacy by design in countering the calls and had failed to respond in time to data subject requests. The objections about Articles 17 and 21 were dropped. The Garante issued a warning, ordered several corrective measures on residential data collection, business sales network controls and handling of rights requests, and fined the company EUR 676,956 (0.5% of the maximum). The decision is published on the Garante's website.
The Danish DPA criticised a processor for setting up unsecure URLs in violation of Article 32(1) GDPR. The URLs were used to screen students' skills at secondary education institutions.

The Garante's press release of 9 June 2023 announced a fine of EUR 7,631,175 on TIM for inadequate oversight of unauthorised call centres working outside its official network, for sometimes inadequate replies to people's rights requests, and for wrongly publishing personal data in public telephone directories without consent. The release adds that on 3 July 2023 the Milan court suspended the enforceability of the decision pending further proceedings.

A complaint was lodged by a municipal employee whose dismissal had been reversed by the court. The municipality then published a council resolution on its online praetorian register (albo pretorio) for 16 days. The resolution reinstated him, identified him only by initials, and described the court case, the reason for dismissal and sick-leave-related health information, so he remained identifiable. The Garante held that this disclosure breached Articles 5, 6 and 9 GDPR and Articles 2-ter and 2-septies(8) of the Italian Privacy Code, and fined the municipality EUR 3,000. No corrective order was made because the document had already been removed.

A patient with cystic fibrosis complained that the Sardinian health authority (ATS, succeeded by the Nuoro local health authority) had published online a document containing his personal and health data, including a medical certificate. The authority explained it was a human error: attachments were scanned together and all published instead of only the necessary document. It de-indexed the data, settled with the complainant and trained staff. The Garante found the dissemination of health data unlawful, with no legal basis, and fined the authority EUR 13,000, ordering publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were ordered because of the quick de-indexing.

The Italian DPA fined an online newspaper €15,000 for publishing detailed medical information of a mafia boss. According to the DPA, the paper went beyond what was necessary and violated human dignity.

After a report from the Guardia di finanza and inspections of four linked companies in the energy telemarketing chain (Mas s.r.l., Mas s.r.l.s., Sesta Impresa s.r.l. and Arnia società cooperativa), the Garante found serious violations. Mas s.r.l. made promotional calls using purchased contact lists with no consent and no privacy notice. It had collected customers' Enel Energia contracts and passed them on without being designated as a processor, and it kept no record of processing activities. It was fined EUR 500,000 (the other companies received EUR 200,000, EUR 300,000 and EUR 800,000). The Garante also banned further promotional processing, ordered confiscation of the unlawfully acquired lists and databases, ordered publication of the decision, and sent it to the competition authority.

The Garante investigated four linked companies selling energy-supply contracts (Enel Energia, Hera Comm) through telemarketing and door-to-door agents, after a Guardia di finanza report. Mas s.r.l.s. bought contact lists from several sellers, including a Facebook seller and a Spanish company, without checking that the data had been collected lawfully or with consent. It passed the lists to Mas s.r.l. without giving data subjects information or obtaining consent. It also processed data without being designated as a processor, did not notify the controller of a sub-processor, and kept no record of processing. The Garante found all the alleged violations established and fined Mas s.r.l.s. EUR 200,000. It banned further promotional processing and ordered confiscation of the unlawfully acquired lists, and ordered publication of the decision.

A lawyer complained that the Ancona Bar Association's legal-aid web portal required lawyers to enter their certified email (PEC) address and its password in order to register and file legal-aid applications. The Garante found that the Bar Association, as controller, processed the PEC credentials and lawyers' data unlawfully, without adequate privacy information and in breach of data protection by design and by default. It fined the Association EUR 20,000, ordered it to remove the link to the existing privacy notice and give proper information within 30 days, and ordered publication of the decision. The Association had suspended the portal and cooperated, and had no prior violations.

A former collaborator of SWG S.p.A. complained that the company changed the credentials of his individual work email account and deactivated his company phone before the agreed end of his contract, leaving him unable to access personal data, including special-category data. The company said it had detected a mass download of about 600 files and acted to protect company assets. The Garante found that the checks and controls carried out on the company devices and account were unlawful, breaching the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle and the duty to inform. It fined the company EUR 15,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

The Garante investigated a telemarketing chain selling electricity and gas contracts for Enel Energia and Hera Comm, after a Guardia di finanza report. Four companies were involved: two Verona companies, one of which bought contact lists from several suppliers without checking how the data had been collected; Sesta Impresa; and the cooperative Arnia, which ran the call centre and data entry and was the hub of the scheme. The Garante found all four responsible for all the contested violations, banned further promotional contacts, use of the lists and databases, and contract data entry, and fined them EUR 200,000 to EUR 800,000 each (EUR 800,000 for Arnia, EUR 1.8 million in total). It also ordered confiscation of the lists and paper forms, publication of the decision and referral to the competition authority. Arnia's appeal ended with a Court of Cassation judgment in favour of the Garante.

A civil society organisation complained about ShareArt, a camera-based system developed by ENEA and tested in Bologna museums, which detected visitors' faces, tracked them and recorded attributes such as gender and age to measure interest in artworks. The Italian DPA found that the City of Bologna, acting through its museum body, had processed visitors' data without a legal basis, given them inadequate information, and failed to put in place a joint-controller arrangement with ENEA. The Authority declared the processing unlawful and issued a reprimand rather than a fine, treating the case as a minor violation.

The Garante had provisionally limited ChatGPT in Italy by urgent presidential decision No 112 of 30 March 2023. After talks with OpenAI, the Garante ordered OpenAI, as controller, under Article 58(2)(d) GDPR to take nine measures. These cover a transparency notice for data subjects (including non-users) under Article 12, rights to object and to rectification or erasure, a legal-basis change for training data, a registration link to the notice, age gating, an age-verification plan and a public information campaign. The Garante suspended the temporary limitation from the date OpenAI complies with measures 1 to 7. The decision makes no finding of infringement and imposes no fine, and the wider investigation remains open.

The Controller did not respond to the first request and delayed to the second. It was ordered to fulfill the request for access of the data subject and to provide the information according to Art. 15 GDPR. The request to levy a fine was rejected.
The Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens reprimanded Nuts Topholding BV for not properly responding to a request for access.
The Icelandic DPA decided that the processing of personal data by the city Kópavogur (controller) was admissible and in accordance with Act No 77 / 2000.

The Belgian DPA held that an employer violated Article 12(5) GDPR when refusing to comply with an access request of a former employee. Although the refusal was justified, the controller should have communicated a more detailed motivation for the refusal.

The Czech DPA imposed a fine of CZK 975,000 (approximately €41,500) on the Czech Ministry of the Interior for the widespread collection of health data of individuals diagnosed with Covid-19 who had been ordered to remain in isolation during the pandemic.

The DPA issued a reprimand against a controller for unnecessarily using a burdensome identity verification method when data subjects requested erasure, such as asking data subjects to provide their order number and price of the last order.

The Italian DPA issued an urgent provisional order against OpenAI L.L.C., the developer and operator of ChatGPT, after media reports and its own check. It found that no information was given to users or to data subjects whose data were collected, that there was no adequate legal basis for collecting and training on personal data, that the data were inaccurate, and that there was no age verification for users under 13. It ordered a temporary limitation of the processing of personal data of data subjects established in Italy, with immediate effect, pending completion of the investigation. No fine was imposed in this decision.
Following a complaint by noyb, the Austrian DPA declared that a “pay or okay” cookie banner on the website of a newspaper was not GDPR compliant in light of the granularity of consent principle.
The Danish DPA orders police authorities to not share speeding ticket data when the ticket in question has been disputed.

After the case was sent back and forth between the state administrator and the DPA, the Norwegian Privacy Appeals Board eventually rejected the data subject's erasure request under Article 17(1)(c) GDPR due to data being stored for archival purposes in the public interest.

The Icelandic DPA found that a person who installed a surveillance camera to prove their neighbors wrong in a dispute about traffic congestion could not rely on legitimate interest since the monitoring was not necessary.

The Icelandic DPA held that by encouraging its staff to evaluate each other's performance in an app after each flight, Icelandair violated the principles of data minimisation, lawfulness, fairness and transparency and should have conducted a prior data protection impact assessment.

The Finnish DPA held that consent requested by the controller for direct marketing in the context of participation in a lottery was freely given in accordance with Article 4(11) GDPR and fulfilled the condition for withdrawal of consent set out in Article 7(3) GDPR.
The Croatian DPA held that a controller had lawfully rejected an access request on the basis of Article 12(2) GDPR, as it was unable to identify the data subject.

Notwithstanding the wording of Articles 15 and 12 GDPR, the Austrian DPA found that the duty to react to an access request is fully independent from the qualification of the addressee as a controller pursuant to Article 4(7) GDPR.

A local health authority in Sardinia emailed a document authorising an out-of-region hospital stay to an email address that did not belong to the patient. The document contained her identity and health information. The employee had attached the wrong note by mistake. The Garante found a breach of Articles 5, 9 and 32 GDPR and fined the authority EUR 4,000, citing the isolated incident, a single data subject, no intent and high cooperation. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased, and the decision is to be published.

A former freelance labour consultant complained that the company's director read and intervened in his work email correspondence on the company account without any notice to staff. The Garante found the company gave no information on email use or shared mailboxes, the monitoring was excessive, and the reciprocal processor appointments with its subsidiary were too generic to meet Article 28. It fined the company EUR 40,000 and ordered publication of the decision. The Article 6 charge was dropped.

The Italian DPA fined the "Ministero degli Interni" because, in activating a procedure aimed at the revocation of a gun license, has divulgated with other public administrations personal and health data of the person concerned.

Following a draft decision submitted by the Dutch DPA under Article 60(3) GDPR, by which the case was dismissed, the Italian DPA adopted the final decision under Article 60(8) GDPR and notified it to the complainant.
Finnish DPA held that a feature that allowed the users of an email service to export their emails one by one did not fulfill the data subject's right to data portability under Article 20 GDPR.
